title: 2 Chronicles 25:14–28
context: Returning from his victory over Edom, Amaziah sets up Edom's gods and worships them. A prophet rebukes him, but the king silences him, and the prophet announces that God has determined to destroy him. Amaziah challenges Joash king of Israel, ignores Joash's parable of the thistle and the cedar, and is defeated at Beth Shemesh. Joash breaks down Jerusalem's wall and plunders the temple. Amaziah later flees a conspiracy and is killed at Lachish. This parallels 2 Kings 14:8–20; the idolatry of verses 14–16 is recorded only in Chronicles.

verses.text: Now after Amaziah had come from the slaughter of the Edomites, he brought the gods of the children of Seir, and set them up to be his gods, and bowed down himself before them and burned incense to them.
verses.arminianNotes: Amaziah sets up the gods of Seir as his gods and worships them. Arminian readers see a sudden and inexplicable choice, a king turning to the gods of a people he had just defeated.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the "not with a perfect heart" of verse 2 now becomes open idolatry. This account is recorded only in Chronicles and explains the disaster that follows.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD’s anger burned against Amaziah, and he sent to him a prophet who said to him, “Why have you sought after the gods of the people, which have not delivered their own people out of your hand?”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD sends a prophet: "Why have you sought after the gods of the people, which have not delivered their own people out of your hand?" Arminian readers see God's patient warning to a straying king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony the prophet exposes. Gods that could not save Edom from Amaziah can hardly save Amaziah, and God's anger burns against such folly.

verses.text: As he talked with him, the king said to him, “Have we made you one of the king’s counselors? Stop! Why should you be struck down?” Then the prophet stopped, and said, “I know that God has determined to destroy you, because you have done this and have not listened to my counsel.”
verses.arminianNotes: The king silences the prophet, who replies, "God has determined to destroy you, because you have done this and have not listened." Arminian readers note that judgment follows the king's refusal to listen.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God's determination is announced together with its grounds: idolatry and refusal to hear. God's decree and Amaziah's responsibility are stated side by side.

verses.text: Then Amaziah king of Judah consulted his advisers, and sent to Joash, the son of Jehoahaz, the son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying, “Come! Let’s look one another in the face.”
verses.arminianNotes: Amaziah consults his advisers and challenges Joash king of Israel. Arminian readers see a proud king freely choosing confrontation, encouraged by counselors rather than by God's word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse parallels 2 Kings 14:8. The Chronicler adds that Amaziah "consulted his advisers," having just refused the counsel of God's prophet.

verses.text: Joash king of Israel sent to Amaziah king of Judah, saying, “The thistle that was in Lebanon sent to the cedar that was in Lebanon, saying, ‘Give your daughter to my son as his wife. Then a wild animal that was in Lebanon passed by and trampled down the thistle.
verses.arminianNotes: Joash replies with a parable of the thistle that asks the cedar for a marriage and is trampled. Arminian readers note the warning in the parable, offering Amaziah another chance to reconsider.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse parallels 2 Kings 14:9. The parable portrays Amaziah as a small power overreaching, warning him that pride invites ruin.

verses.text: You say to yourself that you have struck Edom; and your heart lifts you up to boast. Now stay at home. Why should you meddle with trouble, that you should fall, even you and Judah with you?’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: "Your heart lifts you up to boast. Now stay at home." Arminian readers note that even an enemy king sees Amaziah's pride clearly and urges restraint, a warning Amaziah is free to heed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse parallels 2 Kings 14:10, and that Proverbs 16:18 warns, "Pride goes before destruction." Amaziah's success against Edom has become the root of his downfall.

verses.text: But Amaziah would not listen; for it was of God, that he might deliver them into the hand of their enemies, because they had sought after the gods of Edom.
verses.arminianNotes: "Amaziah would not listen; for it was of God," that Judah might be delivered to its enemies for seeking Edom's gods. Arminian readers note that God's judgment works through Amaziah's own stubborn choice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Chronicler traces Amaziah's refusal to God's purpose in judgment, compare Judges 9:23. Both traditions see the king's responsibility and God's justice affirmed together.

verses.text: So Joash king of Israel went up, and he and Amaziah king of Judah looked one another in the face at Beth Shemesh, which belongs to Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: Joash goes up and meets Amaziah at Beth Shemesh in Judah. Arminian readers note that the challenge Amaziah issued now comes to pass on his own territory.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse parallels 2 Kings 14:11. The battle Amaziah sought comes to him, and the outcome is already determined by God's word in verse 16.

verses.text: Judah was defeated by Israel; so every man fled to his tent.
verses.arminianNotes: Judah is defeated, and every man flees to his tent. Arminian readers see the consequence of a king's pride and idolatry falling on the whole nation he leads.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse parallels 2 Kings 14:12. Judah's defeat fulfills the prophet's warning that God would deliver them for seeking the gods of Edom.

verses.text: Joash king of Israel took Amaziah king of Judah, the son of Joash the son of Jehoahaz, at Beth Shemesh and brought him to Jerusalem, and broke down the wall of Jerusalem from the gate of Ephraim to the corner gate, four hundred cubits.
verses.arminianNotes: Joash captures Amaziah and breaks down four hundred cubits of Jerusalem's wall. Arminian readers note the humiliation of a king taken captive and his capital left exposed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse parallels 2 Kings 14:13. The broken wall of the city God chose is a visible mark of judgment on a king who turned to other gods.

verses.text: He took all the gold and silver, and all the vessels that were found in God’s house with Obed-Edom, and the treasures of the king’s house, and the hostages, and returned to Samaria.
verses.arminianNotes: Joash takes the gold, silver, temple vessels "with Obed-Edom," the palace treasures, and hostages. Arminian readers see the cost of Amaziah's choices borne by the temple and the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse parallels 2 Kings 14:14; the Chronicler adds the mention of Obed-Edom. The treasures of God's house are lost because the king sought other gods.

verses.text: Amaziah the son of Joash, king of Judah, lived for fifteen years after the death of Joash, son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Amaziah lives fifteen years after the death of Joash king of Israel. Arminian readers note that God gives Amaziah many more years, time in which repentance remained possible.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse parallels 2 Kings 14:17. The long years after his defeat show that God's judgment did not end his life at once, though his reign never recovered.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Amaziah, first and last, behold, aren’t they written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel?
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of Amaziah's acts are in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel. Arminian readers note that his reign is remembered for both an obedient beginning and an idolatrous turning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Chronicler refers readers to fuller records. His own account has selected what shows the connection between Amaziah's heart and the course of his reign.

verses.text: Now from the time that Amaziah turned away from following the LORD, they made a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem. He fled to Lachish, but they sent after him to Lachish and killed him there.
verses.arminianNotes: "From the time that Amaziah turned away from following the LORD," a conspiracy forms; he flees to Lachish and is killed. Arminian readers see the Chronicler link his end to his turning away.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Kings 14:19 records the conspiracy and death at Lachish without this explanation. The Chronicler's phrase interprets the event theologically, and the two are allowed to stand side by side.

verses.text: They brought him on horses and buried him with his fathers in the City of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: They bring him back on horses and bury him with his fathers "in the City of Judah." Arminian readers note that, despite his end, he receives a royal burial with his fathers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Kings 14:20 says "in David's city." The wording differs and is noted rather than resolved; both accounts describe a burial among the kings of Judah.
